questions.q: What are the required structural rules for a future method's signature?
options: It must be an instance method that returns a List
It must be a static method, annotated with @future, that returns void
It must be marked public abstract and implement an interface
It must return an Id so the caller can track the job
questions.explain: A future method must be static, annotated with @future, and must return void. It cannot return any value to the caller.

questions.q: Why can't you pass an Account record directly as a parameter to a future method?
options: Future methods can only accept parameters that are primitives, arrays of primitives, or collections of primitives — passing the record's Id and querying fresh data inside the method is the documented workaround
Account is a reserved word in Apex and cannot be used as a type anywhere
Future methods can accept sObjects, but only if the object has fewer than 10 fields
There is no actual restriction — any type can be passed to a future method
questions.explain: Future methods only accept primitive types, arrays of primitives, or collections of primitives. The documented workaround is to pass the record's Id (or a Set/List of Ids) and query for the current record inside the method, avoiding stale data.

questions.q: When is @future(callout=true) required instead of plain @future?
options: Whenever the future method performs an HTTP callout to an external system
Whenever the future method performs a SOQL query
Whenever the future method is called from a Visualforce page
Always — plain @future with no parameters is never valid syntax
questions.explain: A future method that makes an HTTP callout must declare @future(callout=true). Attempting a callout from a future method without that flag throws a runtime error.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of future method calls that can be queued from a single Apex invocation?
options: There is no limit on future method calls per invocation
questions.explain: A single Apex invocation can queue a maximum of 50 future method calls, and that count draws from the same shared daily async Apex limit covered in Lesson 11.

questions.q: Why does Salesforce's current documentation recommend Queueable Apex over future methods for most new development?
options: Future methods have been fully removed from the platform and no longer work
Queueable Apex offers a trackable job ID, support for non-primitive parameter types, and the ability to chain jobs — advantages future methods don't have
Future methods are slower to execute than Queueable jobs in every case
Queueable Apex doesn't count against any governor limits at all
questions.explain: Future methods still work and are valid for simple cases, but Queueable Apex covers the same use cases while adding a trackable job ID, support for complex parameter types like sObjects, and job chaining — which is why it's the recommended default for new work.
